evidence.quote: the road (now CT 183) was part of the stagecoach route between Hartford, Connecticut and Albany, New York.

evidence.claim: Route 183’s scenic section runs through Colebrook center and northwest to North Colebrook, in the hills of northwestern Connecticut.
evidence.quote: After downtown Colebrook, Route 183 runs northwest through the town of Colebrook into the hamlet of North Colebrook

evidence.claim: in the hills of northwestern Connecticut
evidence.quote: The town of Colebrook is located in the hills of northwestern Connecticut

evidence.claim: The village occupies an isolated valley, where a triangular common gathers the church and civic buildings.
evidence.quote: Located in an isolated valley at the Junction of Connecticut Route 183 with Rockwell and Smith Hill Roads

evidence.claim: where a triangular common gathers the church and civic buildings.
evidence.quote: The historic district is centered on the triangular common formed by Route 183, Smith Hill Road, and Thompson Road, with the Greek Revival church (built 1842) at the southern end.  Extending north from the common are a cluster of residential and civic buildings

evidence.claim: The scenic designation begins at Route 182 and ends at Church Hill Avenue.
evidence.quote: At this junction, Route 183 becomes designated as a scenic road, reaching downtown Colebrook.

evidence.claim: The scenic designation begins at Route 182 and ends at Church Hill Avenue.
evidence.quote: The route passes a junction with Route 182 (Stillman Hill Road). At this junction, Route 183 becomes designated as a scenic road

evidence.claim: The scenic designation begins at Route 182 and ends at Church Hill Avenue.

evidence.claim: South of the scenic section, the two-lane approach from Winchester meanders northwest as Coe Street becomes Colebrook Road.
evidence.quote: A two-lane rural area outside of Winchester, Coe Street soon becomes Colebrook Road and meanders to the northwest

evidence.claim: Colebrook center’s principal buildings mostly predate 1880, with later construction concentrated in barns, garages and other secondary structures.
evidence.quote: Most of the principal buildings of the district were built before 1880, with mainly secondary buildings (garages, barns, and other outbuildings) built afterward.

evidence.claim: Part of today’s Route 183 once carried stagecoaches between Hartford and Albany.
evidence.quote: the road (now CT 183) was part of the stagecoach route between Hartford, Connecticut and Albany, New York.

evidence.claim: That traffic helped make the Phelps family’s inn a success; Arah Phelps also sold his farm products there.
evidence.quote: The inn was an economic success as the road (now CT 183) was part of the stagecoach route between Hartford, Connecticut and Albany, New York. In addition to operating the tavern and mill, Arah also sold his own farm products at the inn.

evidence.claim: In 1922, the Winsted-to-state-line route became State Highway 174. Ten years later, the state renumbered it Route 183; the extension south to Torrington followed in 1955.
evidence.quote: The Winsted-Colebrook route, continuing north to the Massachusetts state line, was designated in 1922 as State Highway 174. In the 1932 state highway renumbering, old Highway 174 became Route 183, running from US 44 in Winchester to the state line.  In 1955, it was extended south to Torrington along former SR 710 to the current southern terminus.

evidence.claim: Travel north from Route 182 into Colebrook center, where Route 183 turns northwest at the junction with Rockwell Road.
evidence.quote: In downtown Colebrook, Route 183 turns northwest and into a junction with Route 182A (Rockwell Road).

evidence.claim: The 1812 store faces the town hall; beyond the Samuel Rockwell House, the district slopes toward Center Brook.
evidence.quote: Opposite the town hall is the 1812 Colebrook Store, one of the district's finest examples of Federal period architecture.  North of the store is the Samuel Rockwell House, and beyond that the district descends to Center Brook.

evidence.claim: In northern Colebrook, Phelps family farm buildings occupy land along Route 183 and Prock Hill Road.
evidence.quote: The Phelps Farm Historic District encompasses a collection of farm and residential properties on Connecticut Route 183 and Prock Hill Road in Colebrook, Connecticut.

evidence.claim: In northern Colebrook
evidence.quote: land in northern Colebrook

evidence.claim: Continue toward North Colebrook and the end of the scenic section at Church Hill Avenue.
evidence.quote: where the scenic road designation ends at the junction with Church Hill Avenue.

evidence.claim: A Greek Revival church built in 1842 anchors the south end of Colebrook’s triangular common.
evidence.quote: with the Greek Revival church (built 1842) at the southern end.

evidence.claim: Route 183, Smith Hill Road and Thompson Road form its edges.
evidence.quote: the triangular common formed by Route 183, Smith Hill Road, and Thompson Road

evidence.claim: The town’s limited crop land shaped a nineteenth-century economy of sheep, cattle and related businesses, including tanneries on Center Brook.
evidence.quote: With little land suitable for agriculture, the town's economy in the 19th century was dominated by the raising of sheep and cattle, and the operation of associated businesses such as tanneries, some of which were located just north of the main intersection on Center Brook.

evidence.claim: Most of the district’s principal buildings date from before 1880. Later construction chiefly added garages, barns and other secondary buildings.
evidence.quote: Most of the principal buildings of the district were built before 1880, with mainly secondary buildings (garages, barns, and other outbuildings) built afterward.

evidence.claim: The oldest surviving village house is an ell of the Samuel Rockwell House, north of the store and above Center Brook.
evidence.quote: The oldest surviving house in Colebrook village, an ell to the Samuel Rockwell House

evidence.claim: north of the store and above Center Brook.
evidence.quote: North of the store is the Samuel Rockwell House, and beyond that the district descends to Center Brook.

evidence.claim: The district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1991.
evidence.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1991.

evidence.claim: Four slender Tuscan columns support a two-story temple front at Colebrook Store.
evidence.quote: a two-story Federal temple front, consisting of a fully pedimented gable supported by four slender Tuscan columns.

evidence.claim: Above them, a half-round fan decorates the gable.
evidence.quote: At the center of the gable is a Federal style half-round fan.

evidence.claim: William Swift, a local carpenter who chiefly made bedsteads, built the store in 1812.
evidence.quote: The store was built in 1812 by William Swift, a local carpenter whose principal product was bedsteads.

evidence.claim: The upper doorway once served as a loading entrance, a working detail within the symmetrical facade.
evidence.quote: the facade is symmetrical and covered with flushboarding, with windows flanking doorways on both levels; the second-floor doorway having previously served as a loading entry.

evidence.claim: The clapboarded building stands at the northwest corner of Colebrook Road and Rockwell Road.
evidence.quote: at the northwest corner of Route 183 (Colebrook Road) and Rockwell Road.  It is a 2+1⁄2-story wood-frame structure, with a gabled roof and clapboarded exterior.

evidence.claim: Its gabled roof and half-round ornament belong to the Federal design; inside, nineteenth-century fittings include tin ceilings, hardwood floors and counters.
evidence.quote: Features from that period include hardwood flooring, tin ceilings, and counters.

evidence.claim: Its gabled roof and half-round ornament belong to the Federal design
evidence.quote: Its front is distinguished by a two-story Federal temple front, consisting of a fully pedimented gable supported by four slender Tuscan columns.  At the center of the gable is a Federal style half-round fan.

evidence.claim: Windows flank doorways on both levels of the symmetrical front.
evidence.quote: with windows flanking doorways on both levels

evidence.claim: Open pasture surrounds a cluster of Phelps family buildings along Route 183 and Prock Hill Road.
evidence.quote: Most of the farm is open pastureland.

evidence.claim: Open pasture surrounds a cluster of Phelps family buildings along Route 183 and Prock Hill Road.
evidence.quote: The Phelps Farm Historic District encompasses a collection of farm and residential properties on Connecticut Route 183 and Prock Hill Road

evidence.claim: Arah Phelps dammed Sandy Brook and built a sawmill in the 1780s.
evidence.quote: The farm's history really begins in the 1780s, when Arah Phelps dammed Sandy Brook and built a sawmill.

evidence.claim: The family’s inn served Hartford-to-Albany stagecoach traffic, while Arah sold farm products to its customers.
evidence.quote: In addition to operating the tavern and mill, Arah also sold his own farm products at the inn.

evidence.claim: The family’s inn served Hartford-to-Albany stagecoach traffic
evidence.quote: The inn was an economic success as the road (now CT 183) was part of the stagecoach route between Hartford, Connecticut and Albany, New York.

evidence.claim: His son Edward took over in the 1830s and built many of the surviving farm buildings, including a Gothic Revival cottage for farmhands.
evidence.quote: His son Edward took over the property in the 1830s, and it is during his ownership that many of the surviving farm buildings were constructed.   In addition to the new family house, he also built a fine Gothic Revival cottage as housing for farm hands.

evidence.claim: The former inn is now a private residence.
evidence.quote: It is now a private residence.

evidence.claim: Sandy Brook bounds the property on the west and south, beside pasture and buildings that developed from the family’s milling and farming.
evidence.quote: The property is bounded on the west and south by Sandy Brook
